title: Tail-latency-aware cost presets and spreadsheet walkthrough (draft)
content:
Purpose: Draft a lightweight set of recommended presets and a step-by-step walkthrough for the cost model spreadsheet focused on tail-latency-sensitive workloads. This is meant to be a pragmatic operational checklist that SREs, platform engineers, and customer-facing solutions engineers can copy into customer runbooks or use as starting presets in Redwood Optimize.

Scope: Chat and assistant workloads where 95th/99th percentile latency matters (customer UX), plus a short section describing how to adapt the same sheet for bulk embedding and high-throughput inference. Not a formal benchmark study — operational heuristics + spreadsheet usage patterns.

Executive summary (one-liner): For tail-latency-sensitive workloads, prefer small, progressive batching with KV/prefix caching, conservative dynamic quantization (per-layer sensitivity), and a cost-sensitivity sweep in the spreadsheet that highlights rupture points (where throughput gains start to meaningfully increase p95).

High-level recommendations (quick reference):
- Latency SLO <= 150ms p95: target batch_size 1–2, sequence_limit tuned, KV cache hit threshold >= 30% for warm sessions. Prefer fp16 or lightweight int8 QAT only on non-critical layers.
- Latency SLO 150–400ms p95: batch_size 2–8 progressive (see progressive batching below), aggressive prefix caching, enable token-level KV caching. Int8 dynamic quantization allowed for local-only models; validate quality with eval prompts.
- Throughput-first (p95 unconstrained): batch_size 8–64 depending on GPU memory, aggressive quantization pipeline (mixed int8/4-bit where supported), heavy local caching for repeated prompts.

Key heuristics we use in presets:
1) Progressive batching: increase batch_size in small steps (1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8) and observe p95 uplift at each step rather than jumping to a single large batch. Use a short warm-up window (2 minutes) to stabilize caches between steps.
2) Cache warm-up policy: seed KV cache with the first N messages from user session (N=2 recommended). For streaming chat, keep prefix cache active if model side-outputs are deterministic; fallback to no-cache in high-cardinality prompt families.
3) Quantization safety zones: flag high-sensitivity layers (attention projection layers, first/last transformer blocks) as candidates to remain in fp16 while applying int8 to middle layers. When using 4-bit groupwise quantization, run a quality regression on a 50-sample prompt set with automated scoring.
4) Tail-aware routing: if p95 breaches SLO on a route, degrade to lower-latency model variant (smaller model or lower seq_limit) before switching to higher-cost autoscale.

Spreadsheet walkthrough (columns and intent):
- Inputs tab (user-editable):
  - traffic_profile: tokens/sec, requests/sec, typical prompt length (median & 90th), avg history length.
  - sla_targets: p50/p95/p99 latency targets in ms.
  - cost_params: per-GPU-hour, per-inference fixed overhead (network), token billing if hosted.
  - model_caps: memory per model variant, known kernel speed factor (perf factor).

- Presets tab (single-row-per-preset):
  - preset_name, batch_strategy (none/progressive/fixed), initial_batch, max_batch, kv_cache_on (y/n), quant_profile (fp16/int8/4bit-mixed), seq_limit, warmup_secs, fallback_variant.
  - This tab is where the recommended presets live; each preset maps to an internal name we can map to route config in Redwood Console.

- Perf calc tab (automated outputs):
  - estimated_tokens_per_sec = (model_throughput * batch_size) * kernel_factor adjusted for quantization.
  - estimated_p95 = baseline_p95 * batch_multiplier * cache_penalty. (We keep this intentionally simple: baseline_p95 from observed telemetry, batch_multiplier empirically determined in calibration run).
  - estimated_cost_per_1M_tokens = token_cost_factors + amortized GPU cost.

- Sensitivity sweep tab:
  - Sweep parameters: batch_size, cache_hit_rate, quant_profile.
  - Outputs: delta_cost, delta_p95, cost_per_SLO_point (cost / (1 - violation_rate)). This is the most operationally useful chart to show tradeoffs.

How to run a practical calibration: 6 steps
1) Baseline capture (2–4 hours): collect p50/p95/p99 and request/seq distributions for the route at current config. Save as baseline in Inputs tab.
2) Small-scale progressive batching (30–60 minutes): run progressive steps (1,2,4) with KV cache disabled; populate perf calc calibration factors.
3) Cache-only test (30 minutes): enable KV/prefix cache with batch_size 1, measure cache hit distribution and p95 improvement.
4) Quantization smoke test (2–3 hours): apply quant profile to a staging variant, run the sheet with quant kernel factor and run quality regression. If eval score drop > 1.5% absolute on critical prompts, revert or move to mixed-fp16 strategy.
5) Full sweep (overnight): run the sensitivity sweep grid from the spreadsheet across batch_size x cache_hit_rate x quant_profile (we provide example grid in the sheet).
6) Pick preset + runbook: choose the preset that meets p95 SLO at lowest cost and document the automated fallback policy (reduce batch_size or move to smaller variant on repeated violations).

Preset examples (narrative, not raw JSON):
- chat-ux-lowtail (SLO 120ms p95): progressive, initial_batch=1, max_batch=2, kv_cache_on=partial (only session prefix), quant_profile=fp16, seq_limit=512, fallback=chat-small.
- assistant-mid-slo (SLO 300ms p95): progressive, initial_batch=2, max_batch=8, kv_cache_on=full, quant_profile=int8-middle, seq_limit=1024, fallback=assistant-small.
- batch-embeds-lowcost (throughput): fixed, batch_size=32, kv_cache_off, quant_profile=4-bit-mixed, seq_limit=256, fallback=none (scale capacity instead).

Checklist for shipping a preset into Redwood Console:
- Run the calibration steps and attach the spreadsheet snapshot to the PR.
- Include a 50-prompt eval with pass/fail thresholds and expected token-quality delta.
- Add a console roll-out plan: canary at 10% traffic for 30 minutes, monitor p95 & quality.
- Add an automatic fallback route (smaller model) triggered if p95 > SLO for 5 consecutive minutes.

Open questions and risks:
- How do we quantify user-visible regressions for instrution-following tasks automatically? Need a small human-in-the-loop scoring step for some customers.
- Spot GPU variability: calibration runs must be pinned to similar instance types or kernel versions; otherwise the perf factors drift.
- Cache correctness: for privacy-sensitive workloads, caching may be disabled — we need a separate preset family for zero-cache deployments.

Next actions (short list):
- Convert this draft into a spreadsheet template (Inputs/Presets/PerfCalc/Sweep) and attach to OPT-421. Owner: Priya. Due: 2025-10-01.
- Run 3 customer calibrations (SaaS chat app, docs assistant, embed-heavy search) and add examples to the template. Owner: Evelyn. Due: 2025-11-15.
- Add a test harness PR for automated quality regression checks linked to quant profile changes. Owner: Marco. Due: 2025-12-01.

Notes to reviewer: This doc intentionally keeps the perf model lightweight and pragmatic; the spreadsheet emphasizes actionable knobs and an explicit sweep to surface where small cost increases buy large p95 reductions. Looking for feedback on: recommended warmup_secs, seed size for KV warms (we used 2), and quant safety thresholds (1.5% eval delta currently conservative).

Raw attachments (examples to port into spreadsheet):
- small example grid: batch_sizes = [1,2,4,8], cache_hits = [10,30,50,80], quant_profiles = [fp16,int8,4bit], baseline_p95_ms = 120, kernel_factors = {fp16:1.0,int8:0.85,4bit:0.65}.

End of draft.
